Barnaby was not like other owls. While his brothers and sisters loved the velvety darkness of the night, Barnaby was terrified of it. To him, the night was not a time for hunting or flying; it was a giant, ink-colored blanket that hid monsters, shadows, and mysterious rustles. 

Every evening, as the sun began to dip below the horizon, painting the sky in bruises of purple and orange, Barnaby’s heart would do a little flutter of panic. He would retreat to the very back of his hollow in the great oak tree, wrapping his wings tightly around himself like a feather coat.

"Barnaby," his mother would sigh gently, her eyes shining like gold coins. "The dark is just the world taking a breath. There is nothing to fear."

But Barnaby would just shake his head, burying his beak in his chest.

One chilly autumn evening, a thick, silver fog rolled into the forest. It was so dense that even the moonlight couldn’t pierce through it. From the branches below his hollow, Barnaby heard a soft, pitiful sound. 

*Sniff. Whimper. Sniff.*

Barnaby poked his head out of his hollow, his large, dark eyes straining to see through the gloom. There, sitting on a low branch, was a tiny creature. It looked like a ball of golden fluff with a tail that glowed like a dying ember. It was a baby Firefly-Squirrel, a rare creature of the deep woods. And it was crying.

"Hello?" Barnaby called out, his voice squeaking slightly. "Are you okay?"

The little creature looked up, its glowing tail flickering weakly. "I’m Pip," it sobbed. "I was chasing a falling star, and I got lost. The fog is too thick, and my tail is running out of light. I can't find my way back to the Lantern Tree. And... and I’m scared of the dark!"

Barnaby felt a sudden, deep pang of sympathy. He knew exactly what it felt like to be small and terrified of the shadows. 

"I can help you," Barnaby said. The words came out of his beak before he could stop them. *Wait,* he thought, *me? Help? In the dark?*

"Hop on my back," Barnaby instructed, trying to sound much braver than he felt. 

Pip scrambled up, his warm little body pressing against Barnaby’s feathers. His glowing tail gave off a faint, comforting warmth. 

Barnaby spread his wings. He looked out into the endless, misty blackness. His heart hammered like a woodpecker on a trunk. *For Pip,* he whispered to himself. And with a leap, he dived into the night.

The cool night air rushed past his face. To his surprise, it didn't feel hostile; it felt like a cool silk scarf.

Julian stood in the doorway of a defunct furrier, his hands deep in the pockets of a coat that had belonged to his father when his father was a man who still bought coats. Across the street, the lights of the *Galerie d'Or* were amber and dry. Through the tall pane of glass, Julian could see the small, square frame of *The Orchard*.

It was no larger than a biscuit tin, painted in oils that had cracked into a thousand tiny valleys of dry brown and oxidized green. It was by an artist named Giraud, who had died of the cholera in 1849 without leaving enough money to bury his dog.

Julian had eighty-four dollars in his left pocket and a silver pocket watch with a broken mainspring in his right. He was twenty-eight years old, and he had spent the last five years believing that if he could only look at *The Orchard* for forty minutes without someone asking him if he had an appointment, his life would settle into its proper socket.

He crossed the avenue. A taxi honked, a brief, wet bark that died in the mist.

The brass handle of the gallery door was shaped like a greyhound’s head, cold and sleek. When he entered, the silence of the room met him like a dry towel. The floorboards were wide-planked oak, bleached to the color of salt fish.

"Good afternoon," said the woman behind the desk. She was small, with hair the color of pewter, held in place by two long silver pins that looked like surgical instruments. She did not look up from her ledger, but her pen stopped its scratching.

"I’ve come to see the Giraud," Julian said.

"It is in the small room," she said. "The light is poor today."

"The light is always poor today," Julian said, though he had never been inside before.

The woman raised her eyes then. They were very pale, the blue of skimmed milk. She looked at his boots, which were wet, and then at his collar, which was frayed in the manner of things that have been scrubbed too often with yellow soap.

"The small room is through the arch," she said.

The small room was octagonal. It smelled of old glue and beeswax. There were four pictures on the walls, but Julian did not look at the three that were not *The Orchard*.

He sat on the velvet circular banquette in the center of the room. His knees made a sharp angle in his trousers.

The painting was hung too low, or perhaps the bench was too high, so that he had to lean forward, his elbows on his thighs, his chin almost touching his chest.

The picture showed three pear trees behind a low stone wall. The sky was the color of a wet slate, very much like the sky outside, but Giraud had laid a thin glaze of yellow over the grey, so that the light seemed to be coming from behind the clouds, or perhaps from some source just behind the canvas itself. Her face was only three strokes of a lead-white brush—no eyes, no nose, only the tilt of a neck that suggested she was tired.

Julian looked at the red apron.

The rain had washed the city clean, leaving the pavement glistening like obsidian under the streetlamps. At precisely 9:00 PM, Julian walked into *The Rusty Anchor*, a dimly lit tavern buried in the seaside town’s oldest quarter. 

He wasn't there for a drink. He was there to return something.

Julian sat at the far end of the mahogany bar and placed a small, velvet-lined wooden box on the counter. He ordered a ginger ale and waited. 

Five minutes later, the stool next to him creaked. An elderly woman with silver hair pulled back in a tight bun sat down. She wore a heavy tweed coat that smelled of salt air and old paper. She didn't look at Julian, but she placed her hands on the bar. Her fingers were long, elegant, and bore no rings.

"You have it?" she asked, her voice like dry autumn leaves.

"I do," Julian said softly. He pushed the box toward her.

The woman, whose name was Clara, opened the lid. Inside, resting on the velvet, was a pocket watch. But it wasn’t a normal timepiece. It had no numbers, only intricate, overlapping brass rings, and a single, pearlescent hand that was currently pointing straight up, frozen.

"Does it still work?" Clara asked, a tremor of vulnerability breaking through her cold exterior.

"It does," Julian replied. "But as we agreed, using it has a price. You cannot change the past, Clara. You can only visit it. And for every hour you spend there, you lose a year of your remaining life."

Clara stared at the watch. Fifty years ago, on a rainy night just like this one, she had argued with her sister. They had parted in anger, and her sister had boarded a ship that sank in the harbor hours later. For half a century, the weight of those unspoken words had crushed Clara's spirit.

"I don't have many years left anyway," Clara whispered. She touched the brass casing. "I just need five minutes. Just to tell her I'm sorry. Just to see her smile one last time."

Julian watched her. As the Keeper of the Watch, he had seen many people make this trade. Most sought to undo fortunes lost or empires fallen, but the ones who broke his heart were those who just wanted to say goodbye.

"Five minutes will cost you a month," Julian said gently. "Are you sure?"

"With all my heart."

Clara picked up the watch. Following Julian’s instructions from weeks prior, she wound the stem three times counterclockwise, closed her eyes, and pressed the button on top.

A soft, golden light pulsed from the cracks of the watch casing. The air in the tavern grew warm, and the sound of the rain outside seemed to stretch and slow down until it was completely silent. For Julian, only a second passed. 

But when the light faded, Clara was still sitting next to him. 

Her shoulders, however, were no longer tense. The heavy burden she had carried for fifty years seemed to have evaporated.
